lesson.body:
Think of a wine label like an ID card. The producer (or brand) is who made it. Where it's from is often the biggest clue: a country, a region, or a tighter zone called an appellation — a legally protected area, usually with rules about origin and how the wine is made. Sometimes the grape is listed, like Cabernet or Chardonnay, though many European labels name the place instead and expect you to know the grape.

Two numbers matter: the vintage is the year the grapes were picked, not when it was bottled, and the ABV (alcohol by volume, like 13%) hints at body — higher usually means bolder and riper. Origin, alcohol, and volume are legally required. Other words are vaguer: "reserve" often means little in the US, though in Spain and Italy "Reserva" and "Riserva" are regulated aging tiers.

Here's the relief: you don't need all of it. The place plus the grape (or place plus vintage) already lets you make a good guess.
outcomes: Find who made a wine and where it's from
Explain what the vintage and ABV tell you
Make a good guess from place and grape

deep_notes: The modern appellation took shape in France in the 1930s with the AOC system (appellation d'origine contrôlée, or controlled designation of origin). Its rules can set which grapes are allowed, how much fruit a vineyard may produce and how the wine is made. Across the EU the umbrella term is PDO, protected designation of origin. The producer's name tells a story too: some grow their own grapes, while others, called négociants, are merchants who buy grapes or wine from growers.

Europe is not all place-first. Alsace, in north-east France, has long put the grape on the front label, and German and Austrian labels often show a grape such as Riesling next to the place. The place-first habit works because local rules limit which grapes may be used. White Sancerre, for example, can only be made from Sauvignon Blanc, so the name alone tells a trained reader the grape.

Vintage matters most where the weather changes a lot from year to year, as in Bordeaux or Germany. A cool, wet summer and a hot, dry one can give very different wines from the same vineyard. Many Champagnes blend several years and carry no year at all. The trade calls them non-vintage, or NV. The ABV figure is allowed a little leeway: in the EU, for most still wines, it may be up to half a percentage point off the real strength.

The exact list of must-haves varies by market. In the EU and the US, for example, a label must also say if the wine contains sulphites, a common preservative. Reserva and Riserva come with real minimum ageing times, set by national or regional rules. A red Rioja Reserva, for instance, must age for at least three years before release, with at least one of those years in oak barrels.

deeper.body: French labels often say who bottled the wine. 'Mis en bouteille au château' or 'au domaine' means the estate bottled its own wine, usually from grapes it grew. A négociant is a merchant house that buys grapes or wine from growers and bottles it under its own name. Both can be excellent: several of Burgundy's most famous houses work as négociants.
deeper.title: Who put it in the bottle?

deeper.q: A wine bottled by a négociant is always lower quality than an estate-bottled one.
deeper.why: Both can be excellent. Some of Burgundy's most famous houses are négociants that buy grapes or wine from growers.

deeper.body: ABV can hint at sweetness too. Yeast turns sugar into alcohol, so if fermentation stops early, some sugar stays behind and the alcohol stays low. A Mosel Riesling at around 8% usually has noticeable sweetness. Fermented all the way to dry, the same grapes would give a stronger wine. On a still wine, a very low number is a clue to expect some sugar.
deeper.title: When low alcohol means sweet

opts: The grapes came from very old vines
It spent a long time in oak barrels
deeper.q: A German Riesling shows 8% ABV. What is the most likely reason?
deeper.why: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol. Stop it early and you get less alcohol and some leftover sweetness, a classic Mosel Riesling style.

deeper.body: A grape on the label does not always mean 100% of that grape. In the EU and Australia, a wine named after one grape must usually contain at least 85% of it. Under US federal rules the minimum is 75%. So a Californian Merlot can legally include up to a quarter of other grapes, which winemakers often use to fine-tune the blend.
deeper.title: What a grape name promises

deeper.q: Under US federal rules, which of these blends could be labelled simply as Merlot?
deeper.why: The US minimum is 75% of the named grape, so 100%, 80% and 75% all qualify. At 60%, the wine falls short.

v2.body:
In 1922 archaeologists found the tomb of Tutankhamun, Egypt's young king. Inside were 26 wine jars. Writing on the jars recorded the year, the estate and region the wine came from, and the name of the chief winemaker. One reads, in short: year 5, the Western River, chief winemaker Khaa. More than 3,000 years later, a wine label still answers the same questions.

A label is the wine's **ID card**. It tells you who made the wine, where it is from, when the grapes were picked and, sometimes, which grape is inside. The **producer** is who made it: a person or company, sometimes shown as a brand name and often the biggest name on the front. Some producers grow their own grapes; others buy grapes or wine from growers.

Where it is from is often the biggest clue. The place can be a country, a region inside it, or a tighter zone called an **appellation**: an officially protected place name, usually with rules on where the grapes grow and how the wine is made. Only wines that follow the rules may use the name. France calls its system AOC, and other countries have their own. Chablis is an appellation in the north of Burgundy, a region of France. The tighter the place, the more the label tells you.

Some labels name the grape, like Cabernet or Chardonnay. Many European labels name only the place and expect you to know the grape. Chablis is always Chardonnay, and white Sancerre, from the Loire Valley, is Sauvignon Blanc. Spain's Rioja is usually based on Tempranillo, and Italy's Chianti mainly on Sangiovese.

The **vintage** is the year the grapes were picked, not the year the wine was bottled or sold. A red picked in autumn 2020 might rest in barrel through 2021, be bottled in 2022 and reach the shop in 2023: it is still a 2020. Many Champagnes blend several years and show no year; they are called non-vintage, or **NV**. The **ABV** (alcohol by volume, like 13%) hints at body, how heavy the wine feels: higher usually means riper grapes and a bolder, fuller wine. An 11% wine tends to feel light, a 14.5% one full.

In the EU every bottle must show where the wine is from, its alcohol and its volume (usually 750 ml), and other markets have similar lists. On a US bottle, **Reserve** often means little, and words like Premium are usually just marketing. In Spain and Italy, though, **Reserva** and Riserva are legal ageing levels, with minimum ageing times.

You do not need every word. The place plus the grape, or the place plus the vintage, already lets you make a good guess. A bottle that says Chablis, 2022, 12.5% tells you: Chardonnay, from the 2022 harvest, light to medium in body.
deep_notes: Ancient Egyptians counted years by the king's reign, so year 5 meant the fifth year of Tutankhamun's rule. The Western River was a wine area along a western branch of the Nile. The jars never said what colour the wine was, so in the mid 2000s a team from the University of Barcelona tested the residues inside some of them. They found traces of both red and white wine, the first evidence of white wine in ancient Egypt.

In France, a merchant who buys grapes, juice or wine from growers and bottles it under its own name is called a négociant (say nay-go-SYAHN). Many growers also pool their grapes in a co-operative, which makes and sells the wine for its members. None of these is a mark of quality on its own: several of Burgundy's most famous houses work as négociants, and big and small producers alike can make fine wine.

France built its national appellation system, the AOC (appellation d'origine contrôlée, or controlled designation of origin), in 1935. Across the EU the umbrella term is PDO, protected designation of origin, and Italy and Spain have their own versions, which later lessons in this unit decode. The US has its own kind of named wine area, the AVA, which works rather differently, as the next lesson shows.

Why say white Sancerre? Because Sancerre also makes red and rosé, from Pinot Noir. Rioja works the same way in reverse: it is best known for reds, mostly Tempranillo, but it makes whites too, mainly from a grape called Viura. Chablis, by contrast, is only ever white, and Chianti only red. So when a place makes more than one colour, read the colour too: together, place and colour usually point to one grape.

A year on the label does not mean every grape came from that harvest. In the EU at least 85% must. In the US the minimum is 85%, or 95% when the label names an AVA. Vintage matters most where the weather changes a lot from year to year, as in Bordeaux or Germany: a cool, wet summer and a hot, dry one can give very different wines from the same vineyard.

Alcohol tracks ripeness because yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol: riper grapes carry more sugar, so they can make a stronger wine. That is why warm, sunny places tend to print higher numbers. Two exceptions are worth knowing. Fortified wines such as port are strong because grape spirit was added, and wines that keep some of their sugar can be low in alcohol, as the bonus round explains.

The full EU list is longer than the big three. It also includes the bottler's name, a lot number and allergens such as sulphites, a common preservative. Wines made since 8 December 2023 must also give their energy value on the label and a list of ingredients, often through a QR code on the back. In the US, a wine of 14% or less may say table wine instead of a number, but a health warning is required.

deeper.body: The ABV on a label is allowed to be slightly off. In the EU, for most still wines, the stated figure may differ from the real strength by up to half a percentage point. US rules are looser: for wines of 14% or less, the label may be off by up to 1.5 points, and above 14% by up to 1 point. The margin cannot carry a wine labelled table wine over 14%, though.
deeper.title: The alcohol figure has a margin

deeper.key: US rules allow 1.5 points either way for wines of 14% or less, so 10.5% to 13.5%.
deeper.q: A US wine is labelled 12%. What is the full range of real strengths it may legally have?
deeper.remember: US labels get a wide margin; EU labels a narrow one.
deeper.why: Two US bottles a point apart on the label may be almost the same strength in the glass.

deeper.body: ABV can hint at sweetness too. Yeast turns sugar into alcohol, so if fermentation stops early, some sugar stays behind and the alcohol stays low. Light, sweeter Mosel Rieslings of about 8% are the classic example. Fermented all the way to dry, the same grapes would give a stronger wine. On a still wine, a very low number is a clue to expect some sugar.
deeper.title: When low alcohol means sweet

deeper.key: When fermentation stops early, some sugar is left and the alcohol stays low.
opts: The grapes came from very old vines

deeper.q: A German Riesling shows 8% ABV. What is the most likely reason?
deeper.remember: Low alcohol on a still wine hints at sugar.
deeper.why: Less sugar turned into alcohol means a lighter, sweeter wine, a classic Mosel Riesling style.

deeper.body: Look beside the volume on many bottles and you may spot a small e, the estimated sign. It means the bottle was filled under EU rules for average contents: across a batch, bottles must hold at least 750 ml on average, and only a small share may fall short by more than 15 ml. None may be short by more than twice that. So a single bottle may hold a little less, but the batch as a whole may not.
deeper.title: The little e next to 750 ml

deeper.key: The e means EU average-fill rules: the batch averages at least 750 ml, with only small shortfalls allowed.
opts: The wine was made in Europe
The batch averages at least 750 ml
The bottle is made of recycled glass
deeper.q: What does the small e next to 750 ml on a wine label promise?
deeper.remember: The little e: honest on average, not to the drop.
deeper.why: A single bottle may hold slightly less than the label says, but the whole batch cannot come up short.
